# Transit data (GTFS) and commute time

## TL;DR
- **Confirmed static GTFS zips:** MCTS `https://kamino.mcts.org/gtfs/google_transit.zip` and Madison Metro `http://transitdata.cityofmadison.com/GTFS/mmt_gtfs.zip` (7.3 MB, modified 2026-08-24). Racine RYDE and Janesville are confirmed only through the Mobility Database.
- **GTFS-realtime:** MCTS (`realtime.ridemcts.com/gtfsrt/…`, per Transitland) and Madison (`metromap.cityofmadison.com/gtfsrt/…`) both publish trip updates, vehicle positions and alerts.
- **Licenses aren't open-data licenses.** Both MCTS and Madison grant revocable licenses. MCTS requires a "not sponsored by MCTS" notice plus the data date and valid-through date. Madison limits use to helping transit riders.
- **Commute time:** feed GTFS + an OpenStreetMap `.pbf` into **r5py** (`TravelTimeMatrix`) or **OpenTripPlanner 2**. Precompute it before the demo. Don't route live.

## Key facts
| Dataset | What | Access / API | License / ToS | Refresh | How ERI uses it |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **MCTS** (Milwaukee County) GTFS | Routes, stops, schedules | `https://kamino.mcts.org/gtfs/google_transit.zip`. No key | MCTS Developer Terms: non-exclusive, revocable license. Must say the product isn't sponsored or operated by MTS/MCTS, show the data's last-updated date and valid-through date. No MCTS logos. Downloading means you accept | "In a time and manner decided solely by MTS." Mobility Database's latest copy is dated 2025-05-08, so check `feed_info` or `calendar` dates yourself **(verify current validity)** | Bus commute times for Milwaukee seekers. Powers `near_bus_line` |
| **MCTS GTFS-realtime** | Vehicle positions, trip updates, alerts | `https://realtime.ridemcts.com/gtfsrt/vehicles`, `/trips`, `/alerts` (from the Transitland Atlas record). Key requirement not stated **(verify)** | Same MCTS terms | Live | Optional "next bus" demo. Not needed for matching |
| **Madison Metro** GTFS | Routes, stops, schedules | `http://transitdata.cityofmadison.com/GTFS/mmt_gtfs.zip` (plain http). Service 2026-08-16 to 2026-12-05 | Madison Metro Developer License: revocable, non-transferable, limited to uses "assisting mass transit riders" or promoting transit. City owns the data and derivatives. Optional credit: "Data provided under license granted by City of Madison, WI, Metro Transit." Indemnity clause | Per service change (roughly each semester) **(verify)** | Dane County commute times |
| **Madison Metro GTFS-realtime** and Developer API | Trip updates, alerts, vehicle positions; Bus Tracker API | `https://metromap.cityofmadison.com/gtfsrt/trips`, `/alerts`, `/vehicles`. The Developer (Bus Tracker) API needs a key from metromap.cityofmadison.com/dev-account. Whether GTFS-rt needs a key isn't stated **(verify)** | Same Madison license | Live | Optional |
| **Racine RYDE** GTFS | Racine city bus | Producer URL (via Mobility Database): `https://racine.connexionz.net/rtt/public/utility/gtfs.aspx`. Service 2026-09-06 to 2027-12-31 | License not stated **(verify with City of Racine Transit)** | Mobility Database fetched 2026-09-08 | Racine commute times |
| **Janesville Transit System** GTFS | Janesville bus | `http://data.trilliumtransit.com/gtfs/jts-wi-us/jts-wi-us.zip` (via Mobility Database). Service to 2026-12-10 | License not stated **(verify)** | Fetched 2026-10-16 | Rock County commute times |
| **Kenosha Area Transit** GTFS | Kenosha city bus | Listed on Transitland as operator "City of Kenosha", with a realtime feed mentioned in a Transitland PR. Feed URL not confirmed **(verify)** | **(verify)** | **(verify)** | Kenosha commute times |
| **Waukesha Metro / Waukesha County Transit** GTFS | Waukesha city and county routes | Transitland lists "Waukesha County Transit" (feed `f-dp9k-waukeshacounty~wi~us`), but Transitland blocked our automated read. Feed URL and whether Waukesha Metro is included **(verify)** | **(verify)** | **(verify)** | Waukesha commute times |
| **Beloit Transit System** | Beloit bus | Transitland operator listed. Feed not confirmed **(verify)** | **(verify)** | **(verify)** | Rock County |
| **Mobility Database** (mobilitydatabase.org) and **Transitland** | Catalogs of GTFS and GTFS-rt feeds with history and validation reports | Web. Mobility Database has an API **(verify key needs)**. Transitland pages block bots. The Transitland Atlas is on GitHub | Catalog terms vary. Each feed keeps its agency's license | Mobility Database re-fetches regularly | Find feed URLs and validity dates |

## How it works
- **GTFS static** is a zip of CSVs (`stops.txt`, `routes.txt`, `trips.txt`, `stop_times.txt`, `calendar.txt`…). **GTFS-realtime** is Protocol Buffers with three entity types: trip updates, service alerts and vehicle positions.
- **Simplest "near a bus line" check:** load `stops.txt` and flag a job if a stop is within about 400 m (a quarter mile) of it **(choose and document your threshold)**.
- **Real commute time (r5py):** build `r5py.TransportNetwork(osm_pbf, [gtfs_zip])`, then run `r5py.TravelTimeMatrix(network, origins, destinations, departure=datetime(...), transport_modes=[TRANSIT, WALK])`. The result is a pandas DataFrame with `from_id`, `to_id` and `travel_time` (minutes). r5py needs Java (the R5 engine) **(verify JDK version in the r5py install docs)**.
- **OpenTripPlanner 2** (LGPL-3.0, latest 2.8) builds a graph from GTFS + OSM, serves a trip-planning API and supports GTFS-rt updaters. It's heavier, so use it if you want turn-by-turn itineraries.
- Pick a departure time on a **weekday inside the feed's service dates** (e.g. Tue 2026-11-03 07:30). Feeds expire, and a date outside the calendar returns no transit.

## Caveats and gotchas
- Madison's feed **expires around 2026-12-05**. Re-download after that date.
- Madison's license is limited to rider-assistance purposes and keeps City ownership of derived data. A job matcher that shows commute times to riders fits, but confirm with Metro (mymetrobus@cityofmadison.com) before any commercial reuse.
- The MCTS terms require showing **when the data was last updated and when it's valid through**. Put both in the UI.
- Paratransit (e.g. MCTS Transit Plus) and on-demand services are usually not in GTFS. Don't tell a rider "no transit" when paratransit may serve the trip.
- OSM data is ODbL. See [geography.md](geography.md).

## How ERI / a hackathon tool should use this
- **For the demo:** precompute a `commute_minutes.csv` (seeker ZIP centroid × posting) offline with r5py, and load it in PHP or MySQL. Show "about 35 min by bus (MCTS schedule valid through …)".
- Respect `max_commute_minutes` from `data/job_seekers.csv`, and show the walk distance to the first stop. That matters for mobility disabilities.
- **Must NOT:** promise a trip is accessible (stop-level `wheelchair_boarding` is often blank), use MCTS or Metro logos, or cache realtime data as if it were a schedule.

# Employment and disability law - index

## TL;DR
- These pages explain the rules. They are **not legal advice** for any person. For an individual situation, route to **Disability Rights Wisconsin** (including the Client Assistance Program for DVR disputes), the **EEOC** (1-800-669-4000), the **WI Equal Rights Division** (608-266-6860 Madison / 414-227-4384 Milwaukee), **JAN** (800-526-7234), **WIPA** (1-877-826-1752) for benefits, or an attorney.
- Biggest 2025-2026 changes: the **Section 503 7% goal and CC-305 self-ID were rescinded** (effective 2026-09-21); **WOTC lapsed** for hires after 2025-12-31; DOL **withdrew the 14(c) phase-out proposal** (2025-07-07); **Wisconsin DVR has had a waitlist** since December 2025.

## Key facts
| Topic | Number or date | Page |
|---|---|---|
| ADA employer size | 15+ employees | [ADA Title I](ada-title-i.md) |
| WFEA employer size | 1+ employee | [WFEA](wisconsin-fair-employment-act.md) |
| Discrimination filing deadline (WI) | 300 days (EEOC or ERD; dual-filed) | ADA, WFEA |
| WI FMLA complaint deadline | 30 days | [FMLA and leave](fmla-and-leave.md) |
| Federal FMLA | 50+ employees; 12 months, 1,250 hrs; 12 weeks | FMLA |
| WI FMLA | 50+ permanent employees; 52 weeks, 1,000 hrs; 6/2/2 weeks | FMLA |
| Section 503 | 7% goal and CC-305 rescinded, effective 2026-09-21; threshold $20,000 | [Rehabilitation Act](rehabilitation-act.md) |
| Section 501 goals | 12% / 2% targeted | Rehabilitation Act |

| 14(c) national | 642 certificate holders; 35,534 workers (2025-10-01) | 14(c) |
| Employment First | 2017 Wisconsin Act 178; Wis. Stat. 47.05 | [Employment First](wisconsin-employment-first.md) |
| WOTC | Hires through 2025-12-31 only, unless reauthorized; Form 8850 within 28 days | [Hiring incentives](hiring-incentives-wotc-schedule-a.md) |
| Barrier removal deduction | Up to $15,000/yr | Hiring incentives |

# ADA Title I (employment)

## TL;DR
- Title I covers private employers, state and local governments, employment agencies and unions with **15 or more employees** (each working day in 20+ calendar weeks this year or last). Smaller Wisconsin employers are still covered by the [Wisconsin Fair Employment Act](wisconsin-fair-employment-act.md).
- A "qualified individual" can do the **essential functions** of the job **with or without reasonable accommodation**. The employer must accommodate unless that causes **undue hardship** (significant difficulty or expense).
- Medical questions follow a three-stage rule: **none before a job offer**, broad exams **after a conditional offer** (if everyone in the job category gets them), and only **job-related and consistent with business necessity** questions during employment.
- File a charge with the EEOC within **300 days** in Wisconsin (180 days is the base rule; Wisconsin has a state agency, so 300 applies). Filing with either the EEOC or the WI Equal Rights Division is dual-filed with the other.

## Key facts
| Item | Rule | Citation |
|---|---|---|
| Covered employer | 15+ employees for each working day in 20+ calendar weeks in current or preceding year | 42 U.S.C. 12111(5) |
| Not covered | The U.S. government (see [Section 501](rehabilitation-act.md)), Indian tribes, tax-exempt private membership clubs | 42 U.S.C. 12111(5)(B) |
| Definition of disability | (1) actual disability, (2) record of, (3) regarded as | 29 CFR 1630.2(g) |
| Major life activities | Include working, learning, seeing, and major bodily functions (immune, neurological, endocrine, etc.) | 29 CFR 1630.2(i) |
| Mitigating measures | Ignored when deciding "substantially limits," except ordinary glasses or contacts | 29 CFR 1630.2(j)(1)(vi) |
| Episodic or in remission | Covered if substantially limiting when active | 29 CFR 1630.2(j)(1)(vii) |
| "Transitory and minor" defense | Regarded-as prong only; transitory = 6 months or less, and must also be minor | 29 CFR 1630.15(f) |
| No accommodation duty | For people covered only under "regarded as" | 29 CFR 1630.2(o)(4) |
| Essential functions evidence | Employer judgment, written job description prepared before advertising, time spent, consequences, past incumbents | 42 U.S.C. 12111(8); 29 CFR 1630.2(n) |
| Undue hardship factors | Net cost (after tax credits and outside funding), resources of facility and employer, type of operation, impact | 29 CFR 1630.2(p) |
| Pre-offer inquiries | Prohibited; may ask about ability to do job functions and ask applicant to describe or demonstrate | 29 CFR 1630.13(a), 1630.14(a) |
| Post-offer exams | Allowed if all entering employees in the job category get them | 29 CFR 1630.14(b) |
| During employment | Only if job-related and consistent with business necessity | 29 CFR 1630.14(c) |
| Confidentiality | Separate forms and separate medical files | 42 U.S.C. 12112(d)(3)(B); 29 CFR 1630.14 |
| Retaliation and interference | Prohibited | 29 CFR 1630.12 |
| Charge deadline | 180 days, extended to 300 days where a state agency enforces a similar law (Wisconsin does) | EEOC time limits page |
| Federal employees | Contact agency EEO counselor within 45 days | EEOC time limits page |
| EEOC phones | 1-800-669-4000; TTY 1-800-669-6820; ASL video 1-844-234-5122 | EEOC how-to-file page |
| Nearest office | EEOC Milwaukee Area Office, Reuss Federal Plaza, 310 W. Wisconsin Ave., Suite 500, Milwaukee, WI 53203 | EEOC field office page |

## How it works
**Who is protected.** A person has a disability if an impairment substantially limits a major life activity, if they have a record of one, or if the employer treats them as having one. Since the ADA Amendments Act (effective 2009-01-01), "substantially limits" is read broadly and is "not meant to be a demanding standard." Ignore medication, hearing aids and other mitigating measures when deciding.

**Qualified individual.** The person must meet the job's skill, education and experience requirements and be able to do the essential functions, with or without accommodation. Marginal duties do not count. A job description written before the job was posted is evidence, not the final word.

**Reasonable accommodation.** This is any change to the application process, the work environment, or how the job is done. Examples: job restructuring, modified schedules, equipment, interpreters, leave, and reassignment to a vacant job as a last resort. The employer may pick among effective options and may pick the cheaper one. It cannot force an accommodation on someone who does not want it. It cannot lower pay to cover the cost.

**The interactive process.** A request does not need the words "ADA" or "reasonable accommodation." Plain English is enough, and it can be oral. A family member, friend, health professional or job coach can make it. The request starts an informal dialogue. Ignoring a request or delaying without reason can itself violate the ADA. See [disclosure and accommodation requests](disclosure-and-accommodation-requests.md).

**Documentation.** If the disability or need is not obvious, the employer may ask for documentation limited to showing the disability and the need. It generally may not ask for complete medical records.

**Undue hardship.** Judged case by case against the employer's resources. Cost is measured net of tax credits and outside funding, such as DVR-purchased equipment. Unduly disruptive accommodations, or ones that would fundamentally change the business, can also qualify.

**Medical questions, in three stages.**
1. *Before an offer:* no questions about whether the applicant has a disability or how severe it is, and no medical exams. Asking "Can you do X, with or without accommodation?" is fine.
2. *After a conditional offer, before work starts:* exams and questions are allowed if everyone entering that job category gets them. Withdrawing the offer based on results must be job-related and consistent with business necessity.
3. *During employment:* only job-related and consistent with business necessity. Voluntary wellness programs have their own rules.

**Confidentiality.** Medical information goes on separate forms in a separate medical file. It may be shared only with supervisors (restrictions and accommodations only), first aid and safety staff (if emergency treatment may be needed), and government investigators.

**Retaliation.** It is illegal to punish someone for opposing discrimination, filing a charge, or helping an investigation. It is also illegal to coerce, threaten or interfere with someone using ADA rights, including requesting accommodation.

**Filing.** Charges go through the EEOC Public Portal, by phone intake, in person, by mail, or through the WI Equal Rights Division. Under worksharing agreements, a charge filed with the state agency is dual-filed with the EEOC. Weekends and holidays count toward the deadline, but a deadline falling on one rolls to the next business day. Internal grievances do not stop the clock.

## Caveats and gotchas
- **Use 300 days, but file early.** Ongoing harassment runs from the last incident. Each separate act, such as a firing or a denied promotion, has its own clock.
- **The 2002 accommodation guidance predates the ADAAA.** Its accommodation process content still applies, but its disability-definition discussion is outdated. Use 29 CFR 1630.2 for the definition.
- **Associational discrimination** (being treated badly because of a family member's disability) is covered by the ADA but not by Wisconsin law, per DWD. That matters for workers at employers with 15+ employees.
- **Current illegal drug use** is not protected. People in recovery are.
- Damages caps for ADA compensatory and punitive damages (42 U.S.C. 1981a) scale with employer size **(verify)**; we did not open that source.
- EEOC guidance is not binding law, and federal agency guidance priorities shifted in 2025. Check eeoc.gov for current documents before quoting guidance **(verify)**.

## How ERI / a hackathon tool should use this
- Treat "15+ employees?" as a routing question. Under 15 → Wisconsin law only (ERD). 15+ → both (dual filing).
- Show a **deadline calculator** that counts 300 calendar days from the event date, labeled "estimate." It must tell users to contact the EEOC or ERD promptly and never say they are "out of time."
- Job-matching and intake tools must **not ask employers to collect diagnosis or medical history pre-offer**. Frame screening questions as "Can you perform [function], with or without accommodation?"
- Store any medical or accommodation information **separately** from the general job-seeker profile, with access limited by role.
- A tool must NOT tell someone whether they "have a disability under the ADA" or whether they have a case. Route them to Disability Rights Wisconsin, the EEOC (1-800-669-4000), the WI ERD (608-266-6860), or an attorney.

# AI in hiring, online assessments and disability

## TL;DR
- The ADA applies to hiring tools whether a person or software makes the call. Employers are responsible **even when a vendor built the tool**. Tests must measure **job skills, not impaired sensory, manual or speaking abilities** (DOJ 2022).
- Applicants have a right to **reasonable accommodation in the application process**, including online, video and **timed** assessments, unless it would cause undue hardship (29 CFR 1630.2(o); EEOC).
- The **DOJ's 2022 AI guidance was still posted on ada.gov** when we checked on 2026-10-23. The **EEOC's companion 2022 technical assistance** is widely reported to have been removed from eeoc.gov in January 2025; we could not load it **(verify)**. Removing guidance does not change the ADA itself.
- Multistate employers face local AI laws: **NYC Local Law 144** (bias audits, enforced since 2023-07-05), **Colorado SB24-205** (high-risk AI duties), and **Illinois** laws **(verify)** for Illinois details.

## Key facts
| Item | Rule | Source |
|---|---|---|
| DOJ AI guidance | Dated 2022-05-12; non-binding; still on ada.gov as of 2026-10-23 | ada.gov |
| Who enforces | EEOC for private and federal employers; DOJ for state and local government | ada.gov |
| Vendor tools | Employer responsible for tools from other companies | ada.gov |
| Applicant accommodation | Required for the application process unless undue hardship | 29 CFR 1630.2(o); EEOC 2002 |
| Disability inquiries pre-offer | Prohibited (applies to chatbots, questionnaires, games that elicit medical info) | 29 CFR 1630.13(a) |
| Personality/medical-type tests | A test that is a "medical examination" is barred pre-offer | 29 CFR 1630.13(a) **(verify** application to specific tools) |
| NYC Local Law 144 | Bias audit within 1 year before use; public audit summary; notice to candidates (10 business days); DCWP enforcement from 2023-07-05 | NYC DCWP |
| Colorado SB24-205 | Deployers of high-risk AI: risk management policy, impact assessment, consumer notice; AG enforcement with 60-day cure notice period 2025-07-01 to 2026-06-30 | leg.colorado.gov |
| Colorado effective date | Reported delayed to 2026-06-30 by SB25B-004 **(verify)** | not confirmed |
| Illinois | AI Video Interview Act (820 ILCS 42) and 2024 amendment to the Human Rights Act on AI in employment, effective 2026-01-01 **(verify)** | not opened |

## How it works
**Screen-out.** A tool "screens out" a person with a disability if the disability causes a lower score or rejection, and the person could do the job with or without accommodation. DOJ says tests should measure job skills, or employers should offer accessible alternatives. Illustrative examples (ours, not quoted from the guidance): a video interview scoring speech patterns or eye contact, a game measuring reaction time, a resume filter penalizing employment gaps, a keyboard-only test.

**Accommodation in online assessments.** Applicants can request accommodations such as these (common examples; the right one depends on the person and the test):
- extra time on timed tests, or untimed versions;
- screen-reader-compatible or alternative formats;
- an alternative assessment, such as a live interview or work sample, instead of an automated one;
- permission to use assistive technology;
- a human review of an automated rejection.

DOJ advises employers to tell applicants what technology is used and how they will be evaluated, and to give a clear way to ask for accommodation. EEOC says employers must accommodate the application process even if they doubt they could accommodate the job.

**Medical inquiries by software.** The pre-offer ban on disability questions applies whether a human or a chatbot asks. A tool that asks about health, medications or diagnoses before an offer creates risk.

**Local AI laws.** NYC requires a bias audit within one year before using an automated employment decision tool, a public audit summary, and candidate notice. Colorado's law targets "high-risk" AI that makes consequential decisions; employment decisions are expected to be covered **(verify)**. These laws sit on top of the ADA. They do not replace it.

## Caveats and gotchas
- **Federal guidance changed after January 2025.** E.O. 14173 (2025-01-21) is confirmed in the Federal Register (see [Rehabilitation Act](rehabilitation-act.md)). Later executive orders reportedly told agencies to deprioritize disparate-impact enforcement **(verify)**. **The ADA's screen-out, accommodation and medical-inquiry rules are statutory and still apply.**
- Neither the EEOC nor the DOJ document is binding. Courts decide.
- Wisconsin has no AI-specific hiring law that we found; the WFEA still applies to discriminatory inquiries and tests **(verify)** for 2026 bills.
- Colorado's law has been amended and delayed more than once; recheck before relying on any date.

## How ERI / a hackathon tool should use this
A job-matching or assessment tool built for ERI must:
- **Never use diagnosis, disability type, medications, SSI/SSDI status or benefits as a matching or ranking feature.** Match on skills, interests, preferences, schedule, location, transportation and needed supports, all entered by the job seeker.
- **Never show employers anything medical** without explicit, recorded consent.
- **Avoid proxies**: gaps in work history, typing speed, speech or video analysis, reaction-time games, and "culture fit" scores can screen out people with disabilities.
- **Make every timed element optional or adjustable**, and offer a human alternative.
- **Keep a human in the loop.** The tool suggests; a job developer and the job seeker decide.
- **Be explainable.** Show why a job was suggested in plain language.
- **Log and audit.** Track match rates by group where data is consented, so ERI can spot screen-out. Be cautious about collecting disability data just for auditing.
- **Meet accessibility basics** (WCAG 2.1 AA as a target **(verify)** the standard ERI adopts).
- Route any complaint about an employer's AI tool to the EEOC, the WI ERD, Disability Rights Wisconsin, or an attorney.

## Related pages
- [ADA Title I](ada-title-i.md)
- [Disclosure and accommodation requests](disclosure-and-accommodation-requests.md)
- [Wisconsin Fair Employment Act](wisconsin-fair-employment-act.md)

# Disability disclosure and accommodation requests

## TL;DR
- **Disclosure is the person's choice.** There is no legal duty to disclose. But the employer generally has no duty to accommodate until it knows an accommodation is needed. Most people disclose **when they need an accommodation** (JAN).
- A request can be **plain English, oral or written, at any time**. It does not need the words "ADA." It can come from a **family member, health professional or job coach** (EEOC).
- **Disclose before problems pile up.** Employers do **not** have to rescind discipline or bad reviews that came before the request (JAN).
- **JAN** (askjan.org, 800-526-7234) gives free, confidential accommodation advice to workers, employers and job coaches.

## Key facts
| Item | Rule | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Form of request | Plain English; oral is enough; no magic words | EEOC 2002 guidance |
| Who can ask | The person, or a family member, friend, health professional or other representative | EEOC 2002; EEOC intellectual disabilities guide |
| When | Any time during application or employment | EEOC 2002; JAN Q&A |
| Must the worker ask even if the employer knows? | Generally yes | JAN disclosure article |
| Employer must start on its own only if | It knows of the disability, knows or should know it's causing problems, and knows or should know the disability prevents a request | JAN disclosure article |
| Documentation | Only enough to show the disability and the need; not complete records | EEOC 2002; JAN Q&A |
| No documentation | When disability and need are obvious or already documented | EEOC 2002 |
| Pre-offer, disability obvious or disclosed | Employer may ask whether an accommodation is needed and what type | EEOC intellectual disabilities guide |
| Third parties at interviews | Employer may not ask a job coach or relative anything it couldn't ask the applicant | EEOC intellectual disabilities guide |
| Past discipline | Need not be rescinded | JAN disclosure article |
| Standards | Same performance standards may apply; lowering a standard is not an accommodation | JAN Q&A |
| Response time | No fixed deadline; respond as quickly as possible; unnecessary delay can violate ADA | JAN Q&A; EEOC 2002 |
| Confidentiality | Disclosed medical information must be kept confidential and separate | 29 CFR 1630.14; EEOC intellectual disabilities guide |

## How it works
**Deciding whether and when to disclose.** JAN says the right timing depends on why you are disclosing. Common points:
- *On the application or before an offer:* only if an accommodation is needed for the hiring process, such as an interpreter, extra time on a test, or an accessible format. The employer must accommodate the application process even if it doubts it can accommodate the job.
- *After an offer, before starting:* a common time to arrange start-day accommodations.
- *On the job, when a need arises:* the most common time. JAN advises telling the employer "as soon as possible."
- *When performance or conduct problems are already happening:* JAN's guidance is that the person can explain that the problems are related to a disability and ask for an accommodation. Disclosure does not erase past discipline. For a specific situation, route to JAN, Disability Rights Wisconsin or an attorney.

**What to disclose.** Not just a diagnosis. Explain **how the condition affects the job** and **what would help** (JAN). Usually a diagnosis is not needed in the first request.

**To whom.** A supervisor or HR. If the employer has a written accommodation procedure, follow it too. Telling HR about a condition without linking it to a need does not by itself start the process (JAN).

**How to request: sample language.** Adapted from JAN's letter elements: date, names and addresses, the request, how the condition affects work, suggested accommodations, an invitation to discuss, a requested response time, and a thank-you.

> I am writing to request an accommodation for a medical condition. Because of my condition, [describe effect on work, e.g., "standing for long periods causes increased pain"]. I believe the following could help me do my job: [option 1], [option 2]. I'm open to other ideas. I can provide more information if needed. Could we talk about this in the next week? Thank you.

A written request is optional, but it documents what was asked and when (JAN). JAN suggests keeping a copy.

**What employers can ask.**
- *Pre-offer:* "Can you perform these job functions, with or without accommodation?" and "Show us how." No questions about diagnosis, severity, medications, or leave history.
- *After a request:* reasonable documentation of the disability and the need, if not obvious.
- *During employment:* disability-related questions only if job-related and consistent with business necessity, for example after objective evidence that a condition is affecting performance or safety.

**Job coaches.** EEOC lists a job coach as a possible accommodation. A coach can also help the employer and worker figure out what accommodation is needed. A call from a parent to a supervisor about job problems was treated as a request in an EEOC example.

**Wisconsin.** DWD likewise says the person usually must ask unless the need is obvious, and points employers to JAN.

## Caveats and gotchas
- The EEOC accommodation guidance dates from 2002 and predates the ADAAA. Its process guidance is still the standard reference, but check eeoc.gov for newer documents **(verify)**.
- JAN is technical assistance, not a lawyer. It cannot tell someone whether they have a claim.
- "Disclose" to a VR counselor or ERI job coach is different from disclosing to the employer. The job seeker must consent before ERI shares disability information with an employer **(verify)** against ERI's release-of-information policy and DVR rules.
- Employers may choose among effective accommodations. The worker's preference gets primary consideration but is not guaranteed.

## How ERI / a hackathon tool should use this
- Build a **disclosure planner**: the job seeker picks when (application / offer / on the job / not now), what to share (functional effects, not diagnosis), and who (supervisor / HR / job coach). Save drafts privately.
- Generate a **draft request letter** from the JAN elements, with a "this is not legal advice" note and a JAN link.
- A tool must NOT disclose disability information to an employer without the job seeker's explicit, recorded consent, and must NOT require a diagnosis to generate a letter.
- If a request is denied or ignored, show routes: JAN (800-526-7234), Disability Rights Wisconsin, EEOC (1-800-669-4000), WI ERD (608-266-6860), or an attorney.

# FMLA, Wisconsin FMLA and leave as an accommodation

## TL;DR
- **Federal FMLA:** employers with **50+ employees**. Eligible workers have **12 months** of service, **1,250 hours** in the past 12 months, and work where the employer has 50 employees within 75 miles. They get **12 workweeks** of unpaid, job-protected leave per 12 months (26 for military caregiver leave).
- **Wisconsin FMLA (Wis. Stat. 103.10):** employers with **50+ permanent employees**. Eligible workers have **52 consecutive weeks** and **1,000 hours**. Leave is smaller: **6 weeks** for birth or adoption, **2 weeks** to care for a family member, **2 weeks** for one's own serious health condition, per **calendar year** (8 weeks family leave max).
- The laws **run at the same time**, and the worker gets the more favorable term. Wisconsin complaints go to the ERD within **30 days**.
- **Leave can also be an ADA or WFEA reasonable accommodation**, even when FMLA is used up or doesn't apply, unless it causes undue hardship.

## Key facts
| Item | Federal FMLA | Wisconsin FMLA |
|---|---|---|
| Employer size | 50+ employees in 20+ workweeks (current or prior year); public agencies and schools any size | 50+ permanent employees (DWD: in at least 6 of last 12 months) |
| Service required | 12 months | More than 52 consecutive weeks |
| Hours required | 1,250 in prior 12 months | 1,000 in preceding 52 weeks |
| Worksite rule | 50 employees within 75 miles | None stated |
| Own serious health condition | Within 12 weeks total | 2 weeks |
| Care for family member | Within 12 weeks total (child, parent, spouse) | 2 weeks (child, spouse, domestic partner, parent) |
| Birth / adoption | Within 12 weeks total | 6 weeks, starting within 16 weeks of birth or placement |
| Total cap | 12 weeks (26 military caregiver) | 8 weeks family leave; plus 2 weeks medical |
| Period | 12-month period (employer chooses method) | Calendar year (per DWD) |
| Pay | Unpaid | Unpaid; employee may substitute paid or unpaid employer leave |
| Health insurance | Continued on same terms | Continued on same conditions |
| Complaint | DOL WHD, 1-866-487-9243 | ERD within **30 days** of the action or of learning of it |
| Citation | DOL WHD FMLA page | Wis. Stat. 103.10(1)(c), (2)(c), (3), (4), (5); DWD |

## How it works
**Overlap.** Many Wisconsin workers qualify under both laws. The leave runs concurrently. For each question, apply whichever law is more generous. Once federal leave goes past the Wisconsin amount, only federal terms apply to the rest (DWD). An employer policy or union contract that is more generous applies over both.

**Who gets only one.** Someone with 1,000 but not 1,250 hours may qualify for Wisconsin leave only. Someone at a site with few nearby employees may qualify for Wisconsin leave only, since Wisconsin has no 75-mile rule. Many part-time ERI job seekers fall in these gaps; check both.

**Intermittent leave.** Federal FMLA allows intermittent or reduced-schedule leave when medically necessary. Bonding leave is intermittent only if the employer agrees. Wisconsin leave can be taken in blocks or intermittently (DWD).

**Wisconsin enforcement and remedies.** ERD handles complaints. Remedies include back pay, reinstatement, interest, and attorney fees and costs. Liquidated damages are not available. Other damages may be possible in a separate civil action after the administrative process ends (DWD).

**Leave as a reasonable accommodation.** Under the ADA (EEOC guidance; Wisconsin's WFEA likely treats leave similarly **(verify)**):
- Leave can be an accommodation, including leave beyond FMLA, or for someone who isn't FMLA-eligible.
- Accrued paid leave is used first, then unpaid leave.
- The employer generally must hold the job open unless that would be an undue hardship.
- Penalizing someone for leave taken as an accommodation is retaliation.
- The ADA and FMLA are analyzed separately. Meeting one doesn't satisfy the other.

## Caveats and gotchas
- **Wisconsin's leave is shorter but easier to qualify for.** Don't assume "not FMLA-eligible" means "no leave rights."
- The **30-day Wisconsin deadline is very short**. It is far shorter than the 300-day deadline for discrimination complaints.
- The federal FMLA complaint deadline (generally 2 years, 3 if willful) was not on the page we opened **(verify)** at dol.gov.
- Wisconsin also has a Bone Marrow and Organ Donation Leave law for 50+ employers (mentioned by DWD; not detailed here).
- "Serious health condition" has detailed definitions in both laws that we did not reproduce **(verify)** before applying them to a case.
- Wisconsin has no general state paid family leave program as of 2026-10-23 **(verify)**.

## How ERI / a hackathon tool should use this
- A leave screener can ask: employer size, months worked, hours in the last year, and reason. It can then show "may be eligible for federal FMLA / Wisconsin FMLA / neither," and always add "leave may also be available as a disability accommodation."
- Show the **30-day Wisconsin deadline** prominently whenever someone reports a leave denial or firing after leave.
- A tool must NOT tell someone they are or aren't entitled to leave. Route to the WI ERD (608-266-6860), DOL WHD (1-866-487-9243), Disability Rights Wisconsin, or an attorney.
- Job coaches should help workers document leave requests in writing; see [disclosure and accommodation requests](disclosure-and-accommodation-requests.md).

- [Wisconsin Fair Employment Act](wisconsin-fair-employment-act.md)
- [Disclosure and accommodation requests](disclosure-and-accommodation-requests.md)

# Hiring incentives - WOTC, Schedule A, and accessibility tax benefits

## TL;DR
- **WOTC lapsed.** It covers only workers who **began work on or before 2025-12-31**. It was **not** extended in 2025 legislation, per IRS pages updated in 2026. Wisconsin DWD still accepts applications for 2026 hires and holds them as "pending" in case Congress reauthorizes it retroactively.
- When active, WOTC gives up to **$2,400** for SSI recipients and **VR referrals, including Ticket to Work Employment Network referrals like ERI's**, and up to **$9,600** for some disabled veterans. **Form 8850 must be filed within 28 days of the start date.**
- **Schedule A** (5 CFR 213.3102(u)) lets federal agencies hire people with intellectual, severe physical or psychiatric disabilities **noncompetitively**, with a "Schedule A letter" from a doctor, licensed VR specialist or disability-benefits agency.
- Accessibility tax help for employers: the **Disabled Access Credit** (Form 8826, small businesses) and an **architectural barrier removal deduction of up to $15,000 a year** (any size).

## Key facts
| Item | Value | Citation |
|---|---|---|
| WOTC authorized through | Hires beginning work on or before 2025-12-31 (Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2021) | IRS WOTC page; IRS Form 8850 notice |
| IRS on post-2025 hires | Credit "does not apply to employees who begin work for the employer after December 31, 2025" | IRS Form 8850 notice (updated 2026-03-20) |
| Wisconsin practice | Accepts 2026 applications; status "pending" subject to reauthorization | DWD WOTC page |
| Form 8850 timing | Completed on or before job-offer day; submitted to state agency **within 28 days** of start | IRS WOTC page; DWD |
| Wisconsin submission | eWOTC portal or mail; also ETA Form 9061 (or 9062 from a provider) | DWD WOTC page |
| General rate | 40% of up to $6,000 first-year wages (400+ hours); 25% for 120-399 hours | IRS WOTC page |
| SSI recipient / VR referral | Up to $1,500 (120-399 hrs); up to $2,400 (400+ hrs) | DWD WOTC page |
| Disabled veteran, hired within 1 yr of discharge | Up to $3,000 / $4,800 | DWD WOTC page |
| Disabled veteran, unemployed 6+ months | Up to $6,000 / $9,600 | DWD WOTC page |
| SSI group definition | Received SSI for any month ending in the 60 days before hire | IRS i8850 |
| VR referral definition | Referred after or while receiving services from a state-approved VR agency, a Ticket to Work Employment Network, or the VA | IRS i8850 |
| Claim forms | Form 5884 + 3800 (taxable); 5884-C (tax-exempt, qualified veterans only) | IRS WOTC page |
| WI WOTC contact | 608-266-3131; detwotc@dwd.wisconsin.gov | DWD WOTC page |
| Disabled Access Credit eligibility | Prior-year gross receipts $1 million or less, or 30 or fewer full-time employees | IRS Form 8826 / tax benefits page |
| DAC computation | 50% of eligible expenditures between a minimum and maximum | Form 8826 lines 1-6 |
| Barrier removal deduction | Up to $15,000 a year; any size business | IRS tax benefits page |
| Schedule A conversion | Permanent status possible after 2 years satisfactory service | OPM |
| WI civil service | Agencies may request expanded certification to hire persons with a disability | Wis. Stat. 230.25(1n) |

## How it works
**WOTC (when authorized).** The employer and applicant complete Form 8850 by the day of the job offer. The employer submits it, with ETA 9061, to the state workforce agency within 28 days of the start date. Wisconsin's deadline has "no exceptions." The state certifies whether the worker belongs to a target group. The employer then claims the credit on its tax return. The credit is limited to income tax liability, or for tax-exempt employers, Social Security tax (veterans only). Target groups include TANF, veterans, ex-felons, designated community residents, VR referrals, summer youth, SNAP, SSI, long-term family assistance, and long-term unemployed.

**Why the VR referral group matters to ERI.** People referred by DVR, or by an Employment Network under Ticket to Work, can qualify as VR referrals. SSI recipients qualify separately. ERI can help employers screen, but the employer files.

**Schedule A.** A federal agency may appoint a person with an intellectual disability, severe physical disability, or psychiatric disability without competition. The person gives proof of disability before hiring. It can come from a licensed medical professional, a licensed state or private VR specialist, or any federal, state, D.C. or territorial agency that issues disability benefits. OPM's examples of severe physical disabilities include blindness, deafness, paralysis, missing limbs, epilepsy and dwarfism. After hiring, the person or HR completes SF-256. After two years of satisfactory service the person may convert to permanent status. A DVR counselor may be able to write a Schedule A letter, since a state VR agency is an accepted source; whether a given counselor counts as a "licensed VR specialist" is a question for DVR **(verify)**.

**Wisconsin state jobs.** Wis. Stat. 230.25(1n) lets an agency request expanded certification, adding up to 3 names of persons with a disability, when it is hiring persons with a disability. Disabled veterans have separate certification and noncompetitive appointment rules (230.25(1g), 230.275).

**Disabled Access Credit and barrier deduction.** A small business can claim the nonrefundable Disabled Access Credit each year it spends on eligible access expenditures, which are listed in the Form 8826 instructions (commonly cited examples include interpreters, readers and accessible equipment **(verify)**). Any business can deduct up to $15,000 a year for removing architectural and transportation barriers. Both can be used in the same year. The deduction is then total spending minus the credit.

## Caveats and gotchas
- **Do not assume WOTC was extended in 2025. We found no evidence of that.** IRS pages updated 2026-03-20 and 2026-07-20 still say hires after 2025-12-31 do not qualify. Washington state's 2026-07-20 notice says no reauthorization had been confirmed. Check congress.gov and irs.gov before telling employers anything about 2026 hires **(verify)** that no reauthorization passed between July and October 2026.
- If Congress reauthorizes WOTC retroactively, only applications filed on time (28 days) may count, so employers may want to keep filing. That is DWD's practice, not a guarantee.
- DAC dollar limits: the common figures ($250 minimum, $10,250 maximum, $5,000 maximum credit; IRC 44) did not appear on the IRS pages we opened **(verify)** against the Form 8826 instructions. The deduction section number (IRC 190) also did not appear on the page **(verify)**.
- Schedule A text: we could not open 5 CFR 213.3102(u) on eCFR. Details come from OPM's page **(verify)**. Federal hiring practices changed in 2025; check agency announcements **(verify)**.
- Wisconsin's 230.25(1n) item text was incomplete on the page we opened, and any DPM disability hiring program under it was not opened **(verify)**.

## How ERI / a hackathon tool should use this
- Do not market "$2,400 per hire" to employers for 2026 hires without a reauthorization caveat. Show WOTC as "lapsed; may be reauthorized; file within 28 days to preserve it."
- A tool can generate a WOTC reminder for employers: "Form 8850 due within 28 days of [start date]," counted in calendar days.
- A tool must NOT tell a job seeker's SSI status to an employer without consent. Screening for WOTC reveals target-group membership.
- For federal applicants, offer a Schedule A explainer and "ask your DVR counselor for a Schedule A letter."
- Tax questions go to the employer's tax adviser. ERI does not give tax advice.

# Rehabilitation Act Sections 501, 503 and 504

## TL;DR
- **Section 501:** federal agencies must not discriminate and must take affirmative action. Agencies set goals of **12%** employees with disabilities and **2%** with targeted disabilities in two grade clusters.
- **Section 503:** federal contractors must not discriminate and must take affirmative action. **A final rule published 2026-08-21, effective 2026-09-21, rescinded the 7% utilization goal, the utilization analysis, and the requirement to invite applicants and employees to self-identify (Form CC-305).** Non-discrimination, accommodation, outreach and the written affirmative action program (50+ employees and $50,000+ contract) remain.
- **Section 504:** recipients of federal financial assistance, and federal programs, must not discriminate on the basis of disability. Each funding agency enforces it.

## Key facts
| Item | Rule | Citation |
|---|---|---|
| 501 coverage | Federal executive agencies as employers; each agency's EEO office enforces | DOL ODEP laws page |
| 501 goals | 12% persons with disabilities; 2% targeted disabilities; clusters GS-1 to GS-10 and GS-11 to SES | 29 CFR 1614.203(d)(7) (via Access Board AAP) |
| 503 coverage threshold | Raised from $15,000 to **$20,000** (inflation adjustment) in the 2026 final rule | 91 FR 54482 |
| 503 written AAP | Contractors with 50+ employees and a $50,000+ contract (unchanged) | 91 FR 54482 |
| 503 final rule | Published 2026-08-21; effective **2026-09-21**; part 60-30 removal effective 2026-12-21; RIN 1250-AA18 | 91 FR 54482 |
| Rescinded | 7% utilization goal and analysis (60-741.45); disability self-ID invitation (CC-305); data collection at 60-741.44(k) | 91 FR 54482 |
| Kept | Non-discrimination, reasonable accommodation, recordkeeping, outreach, complaint procedures | 91 FR 54482 |
| Former goal (historic) | 7% per job group (whole workforce if 100 or fewer employees); "not a quota" | 41 CFR 60-741.45 |
| 503 enforcer | DOL Office of Federal Contract Compliance Programs (OFCCP) | DOL ODEP |
| 504 coverage | Federal agencies, programs receiving federal financial assistance, and federally conducted programs | DOL ODEP |
| E.O. 11246 | Revoked by E.O. 14173 on 2025-01-21 (this affects race and sex affirmative action, not Section 503, which is a statute) | 91 FR 54482 |

## How it works
**Section 501 (federal government as employer).** Federal agencies are not covered by ADA Title I. Section 501 does the same job for them, and adds affirmative action. Agencies report progress against the 12% and 2% goals in their annual plans. Federal applicants with disabilities can also be hired noncompetitively under [Schedule A](hiring-incentives-wotc-schedule-a.md). Federal employees use their agency's EEO process. They must contact an EEO counselor within 45 days, not file with the EEOC directly.

**Section 503 (federal contractors).** Contractors and subcontractors above the dollar threshold must include an equal-opportunity clause, not discriminate, provide reasonable accommodation, and do outreach and recruitment. Larger contractors keep a written affirmative action program. Before 2026-09-21, contractors also had to invite applicants and employees to self-identify using Form CC-305, and measure themselves against a 7% goal. DOL's 2026 rule removed both. DOL said the disability inquiry requirement conflicted with ADA limits on asking about disability. Contractors are "no longer required to consider quantitative data" on individuals with disabilities when judging outreach.

**Section 504 (federal funding).** Any program that takes federal money, such as many schools, hospitals, universities, workforce boards, and nonprofits with federal grants, must not exclude or discriminate against qualified people with disabilities. That includes employment. For employment complaints, courts apply ADA Title I standards to 504 claims **(verify: 29 U.S.C. 794(d); not opened)**.

## Caveats and gotchas
- **The 7% goal and CC-305 are outdated material.** Many training decks, vendor pitches and older wiki pages still cite them. As of 2026-09-21 they are rescinded. The eCFR page we opened on 2026-10-23 still displayed the old 60-741.45 text, which probably means eCFR had not yet been updated **(verify)** that eCFR now reflects the rule.
- Contractors may still *choose* to invite voluntary self-identification under other authority. Whether that is allowed, and in what form, is not settled here **(verify)**.
- The DOL ODEP fact page still says "$10,000" for Section 503. It is out of date; the regulatory threshold was $15,000 and is now $20,000.
- Litigation, or further rulemaking, could change Section 503 again. Recheck before 2027-01-15.
- We could not open 29 CFR 1614.203 itself; the 12%/2% figures come from a federal agency plan that cites it **(verify)**.

## How ERI / a hackathon tool should use this
- Business-services outreach to federal contractors should **stop leading with "help you meet your 7% goal."** Lead with outreach obligations, accommodation and talent pipeline value, which still apply.
- A tool must NOT ask job seekers to fill out CC-305-style self-ID forms "for the employer." Disclosure is the job seeker's choice; see [disclosure](disclosure-and-accommodation-requests.md).
- Tag employer records with "federal contractor? (Y/N/unknown)" and "receives federal funds? (Y/N/unknown)" so staff know which laws may apply. Do not auto-determine coverage.
- For federal job seekers, link to the Schedule A page.

## Related pages
- [ADA Title I](ada-title-i.md)
- [Hiring incentives: WOTC and Schedule A](hiring-incentives-wotc-schedule-a.md)
- [WIOA Title IV and VR](wioa-title-iv-and-vr.md) (Title IV of WIOA amended the Rehabilitation Act)

## Sources
- [Federal Register, Section 503 final rule, 2026-08-21](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/08/21/2026-17115/modifications-to-the-regulations-implementing-section-503-of-the-rehabilitation-act-of-1973-as) (accessed 2026-10-23)
- [41 CFR 60-741.45, eCFR](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-41/subtitle-B/chapter-60/part-60-741/subpart-C/section-60-741.45) (accessed 2026-10-23)
- [DOL ODEP, Employment Laws](https://www.dol.gov/odep/pubs/fact/laws.htm) (accessed 2026-10-23)

# Subminimum wage and FLSA Section 14(c)

## TL;DR
- Section 14(c) of the Fair Labor Standards Act lets DOL certify employers to pay workers with disabilities a **productivity-based wage below the federal minimum ($7.25/hour)**.
- DOL proposed phasing out 14(c) on **2024-12-04** (89 FR 96466). **DOL withdrew that proposal effective 2025-07-07** (90 FR 29817), saying it lacked statutory authority. **14(c) remains legal federally.**
- Nationally, as of **2025-10-01**, **642** employers held certificates and reported **35,534** workers paid subminimum wages, down from about 424,000 workers in 2001.
- In Wisconsin, an employer needs **both** a DWD special minimum wage license (DWD 272.09) and a federal 14(c) certificate. A Wisconsin-only certificate count was not available from the sources we opened **(verify)**.

## Key facts
| Item | Value | Citation |
|---|---|---|
| Federal minimum wage | $7.25/hour | DOL WHD NPRM FAQ |
| NPRM published | 2024-12-04, 89 FR 96466 (RIN 1235-AA14) | 90 FR 29817 |
| NPRM comment deadline | 2025-01-17 | DOL WHD NPRM FAQ |
| What NPRM proposed | No new certificates after final rule effective date; existing holders up to 3 years | 90 FR 29817 |
| Withdrawal | Published and effective 2025-07-07; 90 FR 29817-29818 | FR Doc. 2025-12534 |
| Comments received | 17,000+ submissions, 11,000+ unique | 90 FR 29817 |
| Certificate holders | 642 (as of 2025-10-01); 23 pending | WHD FY25 report |
| Workers paid subminimum | 35,534 (most recent quarter as of 2025-10-01) | WHD FY25 report |
| Workers (May 2024) | ~40,579; mean $4.08/hr, median $3.46/hr; ~10% earned $1.00 or less; 11.45 hrs/week avg | DOL WHD NPRM FAQ |
| Who holds certificates (2024) | ~93% community rehabilitation programs; ~4% businesses; ~3% hospitals/residential; <0.5% school programs | DOL WHD NPRM FAQ |
| Primary disability (2024) | ~91% intellectual or developmental disabilities | DOL WHD NPRM FAQ |
| WI state license | DWD special minimum wage license, up to 2 years | DWD 272.09; Wis. Stat. 104.07 |
| WI worker review request | Within 60 days after learning of the action, to ERD | DWD notice |
| Youth limit | Age 24 or younger only after Section 511 steps | 34 CFR Part 397 (WIOA Section 511) |

## How it works
**The certificate.** DOL issues a 14(c) certificate when it is needed to prevent loss of employment opportunities. The worker's pay is set by productivity on the task, compared with experienced workers without disabilities doing similar work nearby, and reviewed periodically.

**Wisconsin's added layer.** Wisconsin's own minimum wage law also applies. To pay below it, a rehabilitation facility or sheltered workshop needs a DWD special minimum wage license. The employer must explain the license terms to each worker, and to a parent or guardian if appropriate, both orally and in writing. Workers can ask for review within 60 days, through the ERD.

**Section 511 interaction.** Since 2016-07-22, youth 24 and younger cannot start subminimum wage work without DVR documentation of transition services, a VR attempt, and career counseling. Everyone paid subminimum wage must get career counseling and referral from DVR every 6 months in the first year, then once a year. See [WIOA and VR](wioa-title-iv-and-vr.md).

**Why DOL withdrew the rule.** DOL read the statute's "shall" as requiring it to issue certificates where needed. It said states ending 14(c) do not change federal duties. It said that falling use does not prove there is no need, and noted commenters' worries about job and service loss. Any new attempt would need a new proposed rule.

**Employment First** policy points the other way: public systems should prioritize CIE. See [Wisconsin Employment First](wisconsin-employment-first.md). Wisconsin's Act 178 plans and reports do not mention 14(c).

## Caveats and gotchas
- **Do not say "14(c) is being phased out."** That was true only as a proposal from 2024-12-04 to 2025-07-07. Federal law has not changed. Congress could still act, and some states have ended subminimum wage under state law **(verify)** current list.
- **Wisconsin count unknown.** WHD's certificate list is a Tableau dashboard filterable by state, which we could not read. Download the crosstab for Wisconsin before citing a number **(verify)**.
- The DWD license page lists license terms that ran through 2018-03-31 and may be stale. Check DWD for current licensees **(verify)**.
- One DPI survey in the Act 178 report found 1% (23) of employed former students with IEPs working in a sheltered workshop or community rehabilitation program. That is not a 14(c) count.

## How ERI / a hackathon tool should use this
- A job-matching tool should treat **subminimum-wage jobs as outside the CIE target**, and must not recommend them.
- For people currently earning subminimum wage, a tool can flag "eligible for career counseling and CIE exploration." It must not pressure anyone or judge their current choice.
- Don't present 14(c) policy as settled. Show "last checked" dates.
- Route wage questions to DOL WHD (1-866-487-9243) or the WI ERD, and route individual situations to Disability Rights Wisconsin.

## Related pages
- [WIOA Title IV and VR](wioa-title-iv-and-vr.md)
- [Wisconsin Employment First](wisconsin-employment-first.md)

## Sources
- [Federal Register, 14(c) NPRM withdrawal, 2025-07-07](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2025-07-07/html/2025-12534.htm) (accessed 2026-10-23)
- [DOL WHD, 14(c) NPRM FAQs](https://www.dol.gov/agencies/whd/workers-with-disabilities/nprm-employment-of-workers-with-disabilities-14c/faqs) (accessed 2026-10-23)
- [DOL WHD, FY25 Annual 14(c) Report to Congress](https://www.dol.gov/sites/dolgov/files/WHD/14c/WHD_FY25_Annual_14(c)_Report_to_Congress.pdf) (accessed 2026-10-23)

# WIOA Title IV, vocational rehabilitation and Wisconsin DVR

## TL;DR
- Title IV of WIOA (signed 2014-07-22) amended the Rehabilitation Act. It funds state VR agencies, which in Wisconsin is **DWD's Division of Vocational Rehabilitation (DVR)**. The goal is **competitive integrated employment (CIE)**: at least minimum wage, the customary wage, benefits, integration, and advancement.
- **Pre-Employment Transition Services (Pre-ETS)** in Wisconsin serve students with disabilities **ages 14-21** (until the 22nd birthday). Students can get Pre-ETS as "potentially eligible" without a full VR application.
- **Section 511** bars 14(c) employers from paying youth **age 24 or younger** subminimum wage unless DVR documents Pre-ETS or transition services, a VR attempt, and career counseling.
- **Wisconsin DVR has been on an Order of Selection waitlist since December 2025.** On 2026-06-02 the Joint Committee on Finance approved more funding, and DVR's goal is to end the waitlist by **2027-06-30**.

## Key facts
| Item | Rule | Citation |
|---|---|---|
| CIE: pay | At least the higher of federal, state or local minimum wage, and not less than the customary wage for similar non-disabled workers | 34 CFR 361.5(c)(9) |
| CIE: benefits | Eligible for the same level of benefits as other employees | 34 CFR 361.5(c)(9) |
| CIE: integration | Community setting; interacts with non-disabled coworkers (not counting supervisors or service providers) like peers | 34 CFR 361.5(c)(9) |
| CIE: advancement | Similar opportunities as non-disabled peers | 34 CFR 361.5(c)(9) |
| CIE: self-employment | Counts if income is comparable to similar non-disabled self-employed people | 34 CFR 361.5(c)(9) |
| Student with a disability | In school; IDEA transition age minimum (state may set lower for Pre-ETS); max age 21; IEP or 504 | 34 CFR 361.5(c)(51) |
| Wisconsin Pre-ETS age | 14-21 (has not reached 22nd birthday) | WI DVR Pre-ETS guide |
| Youth with a disability | Ages 14-24 | 34 CFR 361.5(c)(58) |
| Pre-ETS required activities | Job exploration counseling; work-based learning; counseling on postsecondary enrollment; workplace readiness training; self-advocacy instruction (incl. peer mentoring) | WI DVR Pre-ETS guide; 34 CFR 361.48(a) |
| Section 511 effective | 2016-07-22 | 34 CFR 397; DWD ERD |
| 511 counseling for workers already earning subminimum wage | Every 6 months in the first year, then annually | 34 CFR 397.40(c) |
| 511 schools | Schools may not contract with 14(c) entities to run programs paying subminimum wages | 34 CFR 397.31 |
| 511 documentation | DVR gives documentation to the youth within 45 days (90 days if extenuating) | 34 CFR 397.10(c) |
| WI waitlist start | December 2025 | WI DVR OOS FAQ |
| Funding approved | 2026-06-02 (Joint Committee on Finance) | WI DVR OOS FAQ |
| Waitlist end goal | 2027-06-30 | WI DVR OOS FAQ |
| WI IPE timing | Develop within 90 days of eligibility unless extended | WI DVR Pre-ETS guide |
| Job Center of Wisconsin | 888-258-9966 | WI DVR OOS FAQ |

## How it works
**The VR path.** A person applies to DVR. DVR determines eligibility, assigns an Order of Selection category, and, when the category is open, develops an Individualized Plan for Employment (IPE) with the person. DVR purchases services from vendors like ERI, such as job development, job coaching and supported employment. The case closes after a stable employment outcome.

**Order of Selection (OOS).** When a state VR agency cannot serve everyone, it must serve people with the most significant disabilities first. Wisconsin uses three categories:
- Category 1: most significant disability limitations.
- Category 2: significant limitations.
- Category 3: all other eligible people.

Categories are based on functional limits in seven areas: mobility, communication, self-care, self-direction, interpersonal skills, work tolerance, and work skills. Under the waitlist, new eligible applicants wait. **People who already have an approved IPE keep their services.**

**Pre-ETS during the waitlist.** Students who got documented Pre-ETS *before* their eligibility determination can keep getting Pre-ETS while waitlisted: the five required activities. They cannot get IPE-level services like job coaching, transportation or personal assistance until their category opens. Project SEARCH gets limited services. Adults on the waitlist get no DVR services.

**Potentially eligible students.** A student who meets the student definition and has never been found eligible or ineligible can get Pre-ETS through the PE Request form (DVR-18207-E). School staff can verify disability. A student who needs more than Pre-ETS must apply. DVR advises high school students to refer themselves about two years before leaving school.

**Section 511 (subminimum wage for youth).** Before a 14(c) employer can pay someone 24 or younger less than minimum wage, DVR must document:
1. Pre-ETS or IDEA transition services, and
2. a VR application that ended in ineligibility, or a closed case after a reasonable try with supports (up to 24 months for supported employment goals), and
3. career counseling and information and referral, which may not promote subminimum wage work.

Wisconsin DVR says a student or youth "may not work for subminimum wage without first applying for DVR services." See [subminimum wage 14(c)](subminimum-wage-14c.md).

## Caveats and gotchas
- **Ages differ by purpose.** Pre-ETS: 14-21 in Wisconsin. Section 511 "youth": 14-24. The working-age definition in Wisconsin Employment First: 16+.
- **Waitlist status changes.** The FAQ did not say which categories are currently open. Check DVR before telling anyone how long they will wait **(verify)** current category status.
- The 15% Pre-ETS reservation of federal VR funds (34 CFR 361.65) and the full text of 34 CFR 361.36 (OOS) and 361.48 were not opened on 2026-10-23 **(verify)**.
- Pre-ETS money stops on the student's 22nd birthday or when they leave school, whichever is first.
- People who disagree with a DVR decision can contact the **Client Assistance Program (CAP)**, run by Disability Rights Wisconsin.

## How ERI / a hackathon tool should use this
- A **CIE check** in a job-matching tool can test the five CIE elements: wage ≥ minimum and customary, benefits, integrated setting, advancement. Flag, don't block, roles that fail one element, and send them to a counselor.
- An intake tool can show "You may be able to get Pre-ETS now" for students 14-21, and "DVR has a waitlist; here is what you can still do" for adults.
- A tool must NOT predict someone's OOS category or wait time, or tell anyone they are ineligible. DVR decides. Route disagreements to CAP (Disability Rights Wisconsin).
- A tool must NOT match youth 24 or under to subminimum-wage jobs.

## Related pages
- [Subminimum wage and 14(c)](subminimum-wage-14c.md)
- [Wisconsin Employment First](wisconsin-employment-first.md)
- [Rehabilitation Act](rehabilitation-act.md)
- [Hiring incentives: WOTC and Schedule A](hiring-incentives-wotc-schedule-a.md) (VR referral target group)

# Wisconsin Employment First (2017 Wisconsin Act 178)

## TL;DR
- **2017 Wisconsin Act 178** (2017 Assembly Bill 625; enacted 2018-03-28, published 2018-03-29) created **Wis. Stat. 47.05, "Employment First initiative."**
- Publicly funded programs serving **working-age** people with disabilities (16+, or the transition-services age) must **prioritize competitive integrated employment (CIE)**.
- DWD leads, with DHS and DPI. They must keep a **joint plan with performance improvement targets** (updated at least every two years) and each publish an **annual progress report**.
- The current plan (SFY 2026-27, revised January 2026) and the SFY 2026 report (revised June 2026) **set no numeric CIE targets**. A workgroup is developing an analysis to set them.

## Key facts
| Item | Value | Citation |
|---|---|---|
| Act | 2017 Wisconsin Act 178 (2017 AB 625) | Act 178 |
| Enacted / published | 2018-03-28 / 2018-03-29 | Act 178 |
| Statute created | Wis. Stat. 47.05 | Act 178 |
| CIE definition | Same as federal, 29 U.S.C. 705(5) | Wis. Stat. 47.05 |
| Working age | 16+, including the age a child becomes eligible for transition services | Wis. Stat. 47.05 |
| Lead agency | DWD, assisted by DHS and DPI | Wis. Stat. 47.05 |
| Plan update | At least biennially | Wis. Stat. 47.05 |
| Reports | Each agency, at least annually, public | Wis. Stat. 47.05 |
| Rule limit | Rules may not limit access to or choice of services, including prevocational services, Family Care, Family Care Partnership, IRIS | Wis. Stat. 47.05 |
| SFY 2025 DVR CIE | 3,166 in CIE of 27,865 served | SFY 2026 report |
| SFY 2025 DHS long-term care CIE | 7,976 of 56,794 | SFY 2026 report |
| DVR median wage / hours | $15.00/hr; 20 hrs/week | SFY 2026 report |
| DVR average wage, closed cases | $15.63 (SFY 2023) to $17.21 (as of 2026-04-24) | SFY 2026 report |
| DHS long-term care median | $12.00/hr; 12 hrs/week | SFY 2026 report |
| IPS median (CY 2025) | $14.07/hr; 17.8 hrs/week | SFY 2026 report |

## How it works
**What the law requires.** Act 178 is a policy and accountability law. It does not create a new right for an individual or ban any service. It tells state agencies to:
1. prioritize CIE when supporting working-age people with disabilities in activities outside the home;
2. collaborate under DWD's lead;
3. write a joint plan with specific performance improvement targets and coordination methods;
4. report at least yearly on the plan's targets, the number of people served and the number in CIE, percentage change, average hours and wages, barriers, and regional or county breakdowns where data exist; and
5. publish the plan and reports.

**What it does not do.** It does not end subminimum wage or prevocational services. Rules under it may not limit access to or choice of services.

**The 2026-27 plan.** Three cross-agency targets: raise awareness that work is possible, align state and local services, and prepare students through K-12 career pathways and work-based learning. Agency activities include:
- **DVR:** raise median hourly wages; equitable service for underrepresented groups; more measurable skills gains.
- **DHS:** publish SFY 2020-2025 CIE data; CIE training; update IRIS service definitions for the 2026 waiver renewal; Career Planning and Discovery in CLTS; raise IPS fidelity; new IPS sites each year.
- **DPI:** Transition Improvement Grant; Wisconsin Community on Transition; Youth Apprenticeship and career pathways for students with IEPs.

**The SFY 2026 report.** It covers activity from 2025-07-01 to 2026-06-30. Most outcome data is from July 2023 to June 2025. DVR's CIE-eligible count rose from 22,689 (SFY 2023) to 27,865 (SFY 2025). DVR reported a measurable skills gains rate of 48.1% as of 2026-04-24, against 67.6% for SFY 2025.

## Caveats and gotchas
- **Act number confirmed:** 2017 Wisconsin Act 178. Some sources say "Act 178 of 2018" because it was enacted in 2018.
- **No numeric targets yet.** Do not tell funders that "Wisconsin's CIE goal is X%."
- **Counts are not comparable across agencies.** People can be in more than one system. The report flags the IPS figure as possibly duplicative and says DPI's count fell because of stricter wage-matching.
- DVR wage figures are a mix of medians and averages from different dates. Quote them with their date.
- The DVR waitlist (from December 2025) affects how many people DVR can serve during this plan; see [WIOA and VR](wioa-title-iv-and-vr.md).

## How ERI / a hackathon tool should use this
- Report ERI outcomes in **Act 178 terms**: CIE yes/no, hours per week, hourly wage, and county. That lets ERI data line up with state reporting.
- A dashboard can benchmark ERI placements against the state's published medians ($15.00/hr, 20 hrs for DVR), with the source date shown.
- A tool must NOT present Act 178 as giving an individual a legal right to a job or a particular service. Route service disputes to the Client Assistance Program (Disability Rights Wisconsin) or the relevant agency.

## Related pages
- [WIOA Title IV and VR](wioa-title-iv-and-vr.md)
- [Subminimum wage and 14(c)](subminimum-wage-14c.md)

## Sources
- [2017 Wisconsin Act 178](https://docs.legis.wisconsin.gov/2017/related/acts/178) (accessed 2026-10-23)
- [SFY 2026-27 Biennial Plan](https://dwd.wisconsin.gov/dwd/publications/dvr/pdf/dvr-19635-2026-27-p.pdf) (accessed 2026-10-23)
- [SFY 2026 Annual Report](https://www.dwd.wisconsin.gov/dwd/publications/dvr/pdf/dvr-19625-2026-p.pdf) (accessed 2026-10-23)

# Wisconsin Fair Employment Act (disability, arrest and conviction record)

## TL;DR
- The WFEA applies to **any employer with at least one employee**, plus the state. It covers many workers the ADA misses, since the ADA starts at 15 employees.
- Wisconsin's disability definition is its own: an impairment that **"makes achievement unusually difficult or limits the capacity to work,"** a record of one, or being perceived as having one.
- **Arrest and conviction records are protected classes.** An employer may act on a conviction or pending charge only if its circumstances **"substantially relate"** to the circumstances of the particular job.
- File with the **DWD Equal Rights Division (ERD) within 300 days**. Remedies are back pay (up to 2 years before filing), reinstatement, interest and attorney fees. There are **no emotional-distress or punitive damages**.

## Key facts
| Item | Rule | Citation |
|---|---|---|
| Employer | The state and its agencies, and any person "employing at least one individual" (social club and fraternal exceptions) | Wis. Stat. 111.32(6) |
| Not an "employee" | Someone employed by their own parent, spouse or child | Wis. Stat. 111.32(5) |
| Individual with a disability | Impairment making achievement unusually difficult or limiting capacity to work; record of; perceived as | Wis. Stat. 111.32(8) |
| Arrest record | Includes being questioned, apprehended, arrested, charged or tried | Wis. Stat. 111.32(1) |
| Conviction record | Felony, misdemeanor or other offense, delinquency adjudication, less-than-honorable discharge, probation, fine, prison, parole | Wis. Stat. 111.32(3) |
| Prohibited acts | Refusing to hire, firing, discriminatory ads and inquiries | Wis. Stat. 111.322(1)-(2) |
| Retaliation | For opposing discrimination, filing, testifying or assisting | Wis. Stat. 111.322(3) |
| Arrest inquiries | Generally discrimination; bonding exception | Wis. Stat. 111.335(2)(a) |
| Pending charge | May refuse or suspend if substantially related | Wis. Stat. 111.335(2)(b) |
| Conviction | May refuse or terminate if substantially related; specific exceptions (e.g., unpardoned felons in education agencies, alarm installers) | Wis. Stat. 111.335(3) |
| Filing deadline | 300 days after the alleged discrimination | Wis. Stat. 111.39(1) |
| Back pay limit | Cannot accrue more than 2 years before filing; reduced by interim earnings | Wis. Stat. 111.39(4)(c) |
| ERD Madison | 201 E Washington Ave, Rm A400, Madison WI 53703; 608-266-6860 | ERD contacts |
| ERD Milwaukee | 819 N 6th St, Rm 723, Milwaukee WI 53203; 414-227-4384 | ERD contacts |

## How it works
**Disability.** The test asks whether the impairment makes achievement unusually difficult or limits the capacity to work. DWD notes that alcoholism and drug addiction are disabilities under state law, and that AIDS is covered. A work injury can be a disability. Employers may still apply the same performance standards to everyone and ban drugs and alcohol at work.

**Reasonable accommodation and hardship.** Employers must reasonably accommodate unless that would be a **hardship** on the business. DWD describes hardship as difficult or expensive relative to the employer's size and resources, overly disruptive, or a fundamental change to the business. The worker usually has to ask unless the need is obvious. The worker is entitled to an effective accommodation, not necessarily their preferred one.

**Safety.** An employer may deny a job for safety reasons only with objective or medical evidence of significant risk, and only after considering accommodation, per DWD.

**Arrest and conviction records.**
- Employers generally may **not ask about arrests**, except pending charges.
- They **may ask about pending charges and convictions** if they make clear they will consider them only if substantially related to the job.
- **No blanket bans.** Each job and record must be assessed individually.
- "Substantially related" means some overlap between the circumstances of the offense and the circumstances of the job. DWD's examples: theft and a cashier job are related. Drunk driving is related to truck driving, but probably not to cashiering.
- Coworker or customer preference is not a valid reason. Neither is how upsetting the crime is.
- An employer may refuse to hire someone who **lied** on an application. The reason is dishonesty, not the record. DWD advises answering honestly and offering to explain.
- Licensing agencies have extra duties, including written reasons, a chance to show rehabilitation, and a 30-day determination on request (Wis. Stat. 111.335(4)).

**Complaint process at ERD.**
1. File Form ERD-4206 online (dwd.wisconsin.gov/er/complaints/) or by mail or fax.
2. An Equal Rights Officer investigates. The employer must answer in writing. Mediation and settlement are available at any time.
3. Initial determination: **Probable Cause** (goes to hearing) or **No Probable Cause** (dismissed unless the complainant appeals within the period stated in the determination).
4. Hearing before an Administrative Law Judge. Evidence given to the investigator is not carried over, so everything must be presented again. A lawyer is advisable but not required.
5. Appeals go to the Labor and Industry Review Commission (LIRC), then to circuit court.

**Remedies.** Back pay, reinstatement, lost benefits, interest, attorney fees and costs, cease-and-desist orders and training. Front pay may replace reinstatement in some retaliation cases. **Not available:** compensatory damages for emotional harm, punitive damages, liquidated damages, jury trials, class actions.

## Caveats and gotchas
- **Association is not covered.** Discrimination because of a family member's disability is not covered by state law, per DWD. Use the ADA (15+ employees) for that.
- **Medium confidence on disability text.** We could not open Wis. Stat. 111.34 (the disability section) directly; the site blocked automated access. The accommodation and hardship description comes from DWD ERD pages. Read 111.34 before quoting statutory language **(verify)**.
- We could not open **Wis. Stat. 111.395** to confirm its subject **(verify)**.
- **When the 300 days starts.** DWD pages describe it as 300 days from the action "or from when you became aware of it." The statute says 300 days after the discrimination "occurred." Use the earlier date to be safe **(verify)** with ERD for specific facts.
- Remedies are narrower than federal law. Someone at a 15+ employer may also have ADA rights, including damages; this is a reason to talk with a lawyer about where to file.
- The NPC appeal deadline is short and is stated in the determination letter. Read it the day it arrives.

## How ERI / a hackathon tool should use this
- Use the WFEA as the **default framework for small Wisconsin employers** (1-14 employees).
- Job-matching for people with records: let the job seeker choose whether to record offense types, so a tool can *flag possible "substantially related" questions for a counselor*. A tool must **NOT** decide that a record disqualifies someone, auto-exclude jobs, or tell an employer an offense is "related."
- Offer job seekers a plain-language explainer: "In Wisconsin, employers generally can't ask about arrests, and can only consider convictions related to the job."
- Encourage honest application answers. Never coach someone to hide a conviction.
- Route disputes to ERD (608-266-6860 / 414-227-4384), Disability Rights Wisconsin, or an attorney. Legal Action of Wisconsin or similar may help with record issues **(verify)** current programs.
